text: You find a house you can finally picture yourself living in.
title: A PLACE TO CALL YOUR OWN.

text: There is room for a desk. A kitchen you actually like. A front door you would not have to ask permission to paint.
title: ROOM FOR YOUR LIFE.

text: Then you open the mortgage calculator.
title: THEN YOU OPEN THE CALCULATOR.

text: About fifteen hundred dollars a month.
title: ABOUT $1,500 A MONTH.

text: You compare that number with your rent, look at your savings, and think: Maybe this is possible.
title: MAYBE THIS IS POSSIBLE.

text: But the calculator has answered a smaller question than the one you meant to ask.
title: THE CALCULATOR ANSWERED PART OF IT.

text: It has estimated the payment on the loan.
title: THE PAYMENT ON THE LOAN.

text: You are trying to estimate the life that comes with the house.
title: THE LIFE AROUND THE HOUSE.

text: Those two numbers can be very different.
title: TWO DIFFERENT NUMBERS.

text: Let's follow one fictional buyer, Jamie, through the difference. These are made-up figures for explaining the math, not current mortgage quotes or national averages.
title: MEET JAMIE.

text: Because a home can fit the payment you imagined and still squeeze the budget you actually have.
title: A PAYMENT CAN FIT. A BUDGET CAN STRAIN.

text: Jamie is looking at a three-hundred-thousand-dollar home, with sixty thousand dollars down.
title: START WITH THE PURCHASE.

text: That leaves a two-hundred-forty-thousand-dollar mortgage.
title: WHAT IS ACTUALLY BORROWED.

text: For this example, assume a standard thirty-year fixed loan with a six-point-five-percent interest rate and no fees added to the loan.
title: THE ASSUMED LOAN TERMS.

text: The principal and interest payment is about fifteen hundred seventeen dollars a month.
title: PRINCIPAL + INTEREST.

text: Now add three hundred dollars for property taxes, one hundred twenty-five for homeowners insurance, and seventy-five for an association fee.
title: ADD THE OTHER BILLS.

text: That brings the monthly bills in this example to about two thousand seventeen dollars.
title: THE MONTHLY BILLS.

text: Then Jamie sets aside two hundred fifty dollars a month for maintenance and repairs.
title: KEEP MONEY FOR REPAIRS.

text: Now the housing allocation is about two thousand two hundred sixty-seven dollars.
title: THE HOUSING ALLOCATION.

text: That is seven hundred fifty dollars above the loan payment alone, before utilities.
title: THE GAP BEYOND THE LOAN PAYMENT.

text: Some of that money pays bills. The repair money stays in Jamie's savings until it is needed.
title: SOME IS SPENT. SOME IS SAVED.

text: Every amount here is an assumption. The useful part is separating the categories, so you can replace them with numbers for an actual property.
title: REPLACE THE ASSUMPTIONS.

text: There is an important catch in that calculation.
title: COUNT EACH BILL ONCE.

text: If your quoted mortgage payment already includes taxes and insurance, do not add them again.
title: ALREADY INCLUDED? DO NOT ADD AGAIN.

text: Many borrowers pay those amounts through escrow. The mortgage servicer collects money toward those bills and pays them when they are due.
title: HOW ESCROW WORKS.

text: Escrow changes how the money gets there. It does not make the bills disappear.
title: A DIFFERENT ROUTE. THE SAME BILLS.

text: So a payment labeled principal and interest is different from a payment that includes escrow.
title: LOOK INSIDE THE PAYMENT.

text: An association fee may be paid separately. Maintenance usually needs its own place in the budget.
title: SOME COSTS SIT OUTSIDE IT.

text: For a typical fixed-rate mortgage, the scheduled principal and interest payment stays steady. Property taxes and insurance can change, so the total amount collected can change too.
title: FIXED RATE. CHANGING OTHER COSTS.

text: Depending on the loan, mortgage insurance may also apply. Jamie's example assumes a conventional loan with twenty percent down and no mortgage insurance.
title: CHECK YOUR LOAN TYPE.

text: When you compare offers, compare what each number includes. A smaller number can simply have fewer bills inside it.
title: COMPARE THE SAME CATEGORIES.

text: Now look at the savings account.
title: NOW LOOK AT THE CASH.

text: Suppose Jamie has seventy-five thousand dollars saved.
title: BEFORE THE PURCHASE.

text: The down payment takes sixty thousand.
title: THE DOWN PAYMENT MOVES.

text: Assume another nine thousand dollars covers the other closing amounts, including the fees, prepaid items, and initial escrow funding in this simplified example.
title: THE OTHER CLOSING AMOUNTS.

text: With no credits or earlier deposits in our example, that leaves six thousand dollars.
title: AFTER THE CLOSING AMOUNTS.

text: Then moving and immediate essentials take another two thousand.
title: MOVING AND IMMEDIATE ESSENTIALS.

text: Jamie gets the keys with four thousand dollars left.
title: THE CASH LEFT WITH THE KEYS.

text: The down payment has not vanished. It becomes part of Jamie's equity, subject to what the home is worth and what is owed.
title: THE DOWN PAYMENT STILL HAS VALUE.

text: But it is no longer cash sitting in the bank.
title: EQUITY IS NOT CASH IN THE BANK.

text: And prepaid taxes or insurance are money paid ahead, not an extra copy of the same expense.
title: PAID AHEAD IS NOT PAID TWICE.

text: The question is whether Jamie can handle the next bill without borrowing again.
title: CAN YOU HANDLE THE NEXT BILL?

text: Passing the closing-day test and having enough breathing room after closing are two different achievements.
title: GETTING THE KEYS IS ONE TEST.

text: In the first month, nothing breaks.
title: MONTH ONE. NOTHING BREAKS.

text: In the second month, nothing breaks.
title: MONTH TWO. STILL QUIET.

text: It is tempting to decide that the repair category was too cautious.
title: DO I REALLY NEED THIS FUND?

text: Then an appliance fails.
title: THEN SOMETHING BREAKS.

text: Let's use a hypothetical three-thousand-dollar repair. That is a storytelling example, not a quote for any particular job.
title: A HYPOTHETICAL REPAIR.

text: Saving two hundred fifty dollars a month produces three thousand dollars after twelve months, before any withdrawals or interest.
title: A YEAR OF MONTHLY TRANSFERS.

text: But a bill can arrive in month two.
title: BUT THE BILL CAN ARRIVE EARLY.

text: At that point, only five hundred dollars has accumulated from those monthly transfers.
title: ONLY TWO TRANSFERS SO FAR.

text: The rest has to come from money already available, or another source.
title: THE GAP NEEDS ANOTHER SOURCE.

text: That is why a repair allowance and a starting cash cushion do different jobs.
title: TWO DIFFERENT JOBS.

text: The allowance prepares for costs over time. The cushion helps when the timing is bad.
title: BUILD OVER TIME. HAVE CASH READY.

text: And if you spend from that repair fund, do not count the same money twice: once when saving it, then again as a separate addition to the budget when paying the bill.
title: THE SAME MONEY. COUNT IT ONCE.

text: There is another number that can make the decision look easier: equity.
title: EQUITY CAN LOOK REASSURING.

text: Equity matters. Paying down principal reduces the debt on the home.
title: PRINCIPAL REDUCES THE DEBT.

text: But the entire mortgage payment does not become equity.
title: THE WHOLE PAYMENT IS NOT EQUITY.

text: In Jamie's example, the first month's interest is thirteen hundred dollars. About two hundred seventeen dollars of the scheduled loan payment reduces principal.
title: THE FIRST MONTH, SPLIT APART.

text: The exact split changes over time.
title: THE SPLIT CHANGES OVER TIME.

text: Taxes, insurance, and association fees do not pay down that loan.
title: THESE DO NOT REDUCE THE LOAN.

text: And a higher estimated home value does not put spendable cash in the checking account.
title: HOME VALUE IS NOT SPENDABLE CASH.

text: Accessing equity can require selling or qualifying for another loan, with costs and risks. Future price gains are not guaranteed.
title: ACCESS CAN HAVE COSTS AND RISKS.

text: You can make progress on a balance sheet and still struggle with a bill due Friday.
title: A BILL CAN STILL BE DUE FRIDAY.

text: So keep track of both: the wealth you may be building in the home, and the cash you can actually use.
title: TRACK BOTH SIDES.

text: They answer different questions about financial security.
title: TWO QUESTIONS ABOUT SECURITY.

text: Before choosing the house, try building a month around the complete number.
title: BUILD A MONTH AROUND THE HOUSE.

text: Start with take-home pay.
title: START WITH TAKE-HOME PAY.

text: Subtract the housing bills, a realistic repair allowance, utilities, food, transportation, debt payments, and the other expenses of your household.
title: INCLUDE THE REST OF YOUR LIFE.

text: Then look at what remains for saving, emergencies, and the things you want your life to include.
title: WHAT IS LEFT AFTER THE BILLS?

text: Use actual insurance quotes and local tax information where possible. Read the association documents and consider what the inspection tells you about upcoming work.
title: USE INFORMATION FOR THIS PROPERTY.

text: The Loan Estimate helps separate the loan payment, escrow, other charges, and estimated cash needed to close. The Closing Disclosure lets you check the final figures.
title: READ THE TWO DISCLOSURES.

text: Then test a less comfortable month.
title: TRY A TOUGHER MONTH.

text: What if an insurance bill rises? What if a repair comes early? What if income falls?
title: WHAT IF ONE THING CHANGES?

text: You do not need to pretend every bad event will happen together.
title: TEST SCENARIOS SEPARATELY.

text: You need to see which changes would leave you without a workable response.
title: KEEP A WORKABLE RESPONSE.

text: A house can offer stability, control, and a place you want to stay.
title: THE BENEFITS MATTER TOO.

text: Those benefits belong in the decision too.
title: PUT THOSE BENEFITS IN THE DECISION.

text: But they are easier to enjoy when the budget leaves room for the rest of your life.
title: LEAVE ROOM FOR THE REST OF LIFE.

text: For one buyer, that may mean a smaller property. For another, more time to save. Someone else may find that the full cost fits comfortably.
title: DIFFERENT BUYERS. DIFFERENT CHOICES.

text: There is no single down payment or repair allowance that makes every home affordable.
title: NO SINGLE NUMBER FITS EVERYONE.

text: There is a better question than asking whether the loan payment fits.
title: ASK A BIGGER QUESTION.

text: After the bills are paid, after money is set aside for upkeep, and after the purchase is complete, what choices do you still have?
title: WHAT CHOICES DO YOU STILL HAVE?

text: Can you repair the house without immediately creating another payment?
title: REPAIR WITHOUT ANOTHER PAYMENT?

text: Can you keep saving?
title: CAN YOU KEEP SAVING?

text: Can you live there without every ordinary expense feeling like a setback?
title: ROOM FOR AN ORDINARY LIFE.

text: The mortgage payment is where the calculation starts.
title: THE CALCULATION STARTS HERE.

text: The room you have left is what tells you whether the home fits.
title: THE ROOM YOU HAVE LEFT.
